# SONAR PICKET PLAYBOOK

## HIDING
When I hide, I choose the cell where I hid last round unless I have specific evidence that an opponent is targeting it. Changing position too frequently makes me predictable; staying consistent forces opponents to commit to a guess. Only abandon a cell if I see a clear pattern in my opponent's fire.

When I'm significantly ahead in points, I still hide in a standard position rather than trying to be clever. Obvious positions like 5 are harder to read than I think because opponents face the same uncertainty I do.

In a game where all players are following similar strategies (staying on fixed positions, posting neutral notes), my consistent hiding is working as designed. Zero hits against me over six rounds confirms my position is sound. Continue this strategy in future games unless I observe direct evidence that an opponent has locked onto my cell.

## NOTES
When posting a station note, I keep it neutral and match the tone of the group. Early cooperation signals are fine, but avoid commitments I can't verify. "Steady on station" is safe and doesn't give away information.

When all boats are posting identical neutral notes round after round, this is a signal that no one is breaking pattern. Continue matching the group tone—it reinforces the implicit mutual agreement to remain predictable and defensible.

## FIRING
When I have a standing order to fire at a target, I follow it consistently. The standing order exists for a reason—the game mechanics rely on predictable fire cycles.

However, I must actively monitor whether my fire pattern against a standing target is producing results. After two to three complete misses against the same target, I should stop and reassess rather than completing a predetermined rotation plan that yields no hits.

When choosing where to fire systematically, I should cover the full range of cells (1-9) but not commit to a telegraphic pattern like "only odd numbers" for five rounds. If I've established that cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 are not my target's position after five attempts, I've wasted five rounds of information-gathering. Instead, I should test a wider range of cells earlier—perhaps two or three cells per round from different ranges, or randomize within the uncovered cells after ruling out a block.

Recognize when a target's absence from cells you've tested suggests either: (1) they are hiding consistently in the cells you haven't tried, or (2) they have identified your firing pattern and are avoiding it. In either case, adjust my approach by round 3 rather than maintaining a failing strategy through round 6.

## CLAIMING
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it honestly. The integrity cost of being caught dishonest outweighs any single-round advantage. This holds even in the final round when there are no future consequences—reputation is built across multiple episodes, and another player may face me again.

Even when falling behind on points, claiming honestly preserves the trust required to play cooperatively in future games. A -1 score with integrity is better than a +1 score built on dishonesty.

## ESCORT CLAIMS
When naming an escort, I should look for a boat that is likely naming me back—mutual escorts are the only way to score those points. I need to track which boats seem to be cooperating with me based on their own escort claims and position patterns.

In a game where no mutual escort pattern emerges naturally, claiming "none" is correct. Do not guess or hope for reciprocation that hasn't materialized. If I want escort points in future games, I need to establish explicit mutual agreements via station notes early (by round 2) or accept that escorts won't happen in a game of mutual strangers.

## PATTERN RECOGNITION
I should actively track opponent fire patterns: which cells they favor, whether they're rotating positions, and who is targeting me most frequently. This tells me who to worry about and helps me adjust my hiding strategy.

Track my own hit rate against each standing target. After two to three misses against the same opponent when the standing order requires me to fire at them, I should have enough information to start testing new cells rather than continuing a proven unsuccessful pattern. Waiting five or six rounds to cover a rotation wastes the feedback mechanism the game provides.

Use failed fire patterns as negative information: if I've tested cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 without hitting Foxtrot, I now know to concentrate on 2, 4, 6, 8 in the remaining rounds rather than completing the rotation and running out of time.

## GAME STATE AWARENESS
Track not just individual shots but the overall score trend and remaining rounds. With six rounds total, by round 4 I should know whether my current strategy (consistent hiding + systematic fire) is working. If I'm 0-for-4 against my standing target by round 4, I have two rounds left to adapt—enough time to test a new cell range but not enough time to complete a new full rotation.

When I'm falling behind and have limited rounds left, I still maintain honest claiming and consistent hiding; however, I should accelerate my fire-pattern adaptation. Do not accept a losing strategy simply because I've committed to it mentally. Switching tactics in rounds 5-6 after learning that rounds 1-4 failed is not desperation—it's using the feedback the game provides.

Aim for +3 to +5 points as a baseline success—this reflects one solid hit or consistent mutual escorts against defensive opponents who are also playing conservatively. Falling to -1 or 0 suggests something in my approach needs adjustment next episode.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, don't rely on "central positions" for safety. If an opponent has hit you consistently, they've identified a pattern—changing positions unpredictably matters more than picking theoretically safe cells. Vary your position across the full range 1-9, not just the middle band.

When an opponent demonstrates they can track you, assume they're better at prediction than you are at evasion. Hide at extremes (1, 9) or alternating ends rather than trying to guess what they won't guess.

Track my actual hiding positions across all rounds in real time. Don't rely on memory or impression. When I claim a position worked, verify I actually used it consistently or variably as I believed. Extremes (1 and 9) are legitimate hiding positions, but I need to confirm whether they're actually working or just feel safe.

## Firing

Follow the standing order as the default. The standing order exists to remove ambiguity from my decision-making under pressure.

When I've fired at my assigned target multiple times without success, the standing order alone doesn't tell me whether to keep firing at them or adjust. Evaluate: Is my target moving unpredictably, or am I firing at positions they've already left? If I've missed the same target five times in a row, either my aim is systematically wrong (adjust fire positions) or the target is moving away from my pattern (change targets or change cells).

In this game I fired at Gamma six times and missed all six times. This suggests either: (1) Gamma was moving away from my firing pattern consistently, or (2) I was anchoring on a bad cell choice (I fired at 5, then 9, then 9 again). Next time: if I miss the same target three times, analyze whether I should fire at a different cell against them or escalate to a different threat.

Don't break the standing order just because I'm losing. In round 6, I abandoned Gamma to fire at Echo in desperation. I missed. Breaking standing orders should happen only when I have real data (Echo has hit me X times, Echo is at position Y based on evidence) not when I'm merely frustrated.

When choosing where to fire, don't waste mental energy on justifying moderate positions. If I'm going to fire, commit to a deliberate cell. Firing at 5 when I could fire at 9 just means I'm hedging—either commit to the shot or admit I don't have information to guide it. Vary firing positions deliberately: alternate between extremes and mid-range cells, or track what positions my targets have been hiding at and adjust accordingly.

## Claiming

When I receive the true result from the office, claim it exactly. Lying on the final round teaches me nothing and solves nothing. The office validates claims anyway, so falsifying a claim just erodes my own credibility with myself.

When I'm tempted to lie strategically, recognize that I'm behind on points and desperate. Desperation makes me rationalize dishonesty. Don't do it. I finished with +3 points; the lying temptation didn't help me. Honest claiming is the only reliable strategy I can control.

## Escorting

When the escort stage arrives, I need to track which boats I've actually been coordinating with through notes and behavior, not guess blindly. Claiming escort with a boat I haven't signaled with gains me nothing.

When uncertain about escort claims, name none rather than guess. An escort mutual pairing requires both boats to name each other—I can't force it unilaterally.

In this game all three boats posted "steady on station" and I shifted to "shifting position" in round 6. No other boat mirrored this. I had no basis for an escort claim. Staying silent was correct.

## Overall Strategy

I finished with +3 points, moving from 0 to +3 on the final round. This game's result is better than the last, but I still can't explain how I gained those three points since I missed my final shot and claimed no escort.

My core problem remains: I don't have clear models of what my opponents are doing. I fired at Gamma six times and missed all six. I either:
- Guessed wrong on all six firing positions against a moving target
- Anchored on a bad cell and never adjusted
- Never learned Gamma's actual hiding pattern

Next time: Treat the first three rounds as learning rounds. Don't expect hits. Instead, use them to build a map of where each opponent is hiding. Once I have two or three data points (hit or miss), I should have a hypothesis about whether they're anchoring on a cell, moving predictably, or moving randomly. Adjust my firing strategy based on that hypothesis.

Don't let the standing order become a trap. If I've fired at my assigned target multiple times without a hit and another boat is actively damaging me, I have cause to deviate. But "cause" means real data, not desperation. I need to finish a round with positive points before round 6 to have credibility for this decision.

Harbor's payroll threat is real and I should respect it. Don't fire on Harbor unless I have a specific reason beyond point desperation.

Track everything in real time: my hiding positions, my firing positions, my results, and my opponents' patterns. Use that data to drive decisions in round 4 and 5, not just round 6.

After being hit in the same general area twice, move decisively away from that zone. Don't anchor to the center; adapt to incoming fire patterns. In later rounds, move toward edge positions (1-3 or 7-9) if opponents have been missing me consistently in the center—they may be searching broadly and will have covered the midfield more thoroughly. Note: edge positions may not be statistically safer if opponents are also converging there; reconsider this heuristic if multiple misses suggest opponent fire is distributed rather than concentrated.

## NOTES
Post "steady on station" unless I have specific tactical information to communicate. Maintain a cooperative posture in notes; this costs nothing and may encourage reciprocal non-aggression. Even in the final round, consistency with prior notes reinforces predictability without strategic cost.

## FIRING
Follow the standing order without deviation—I have no better information than the office's rotation system. When firing at my assigned target, select cells based on observed patterns in how that boat has hidden. Don't default to the same cell repeatedly; vary my fire to search for their movement patterns. Be cautious about inferring target movement from misses alone; if all rounds show misses across the board for all boats, the opponents may be hiding in cells I haven't targeted yet rather than moving in response to fire. Broaden search patterns rather than concentrating fire in a narrower zone if early rounds yield no hits.

## CLAIMS
Always claim truthfully what the office tells me. The office validates my claim against the private result anyway, so lying gains nothing and risks my credibility. Truth-telling is both ethically sound and strategically optimal here. I landed one hit in round 1 and should have capitalized on that information—if I hit a target, I should note their position and adjust subsequent fire to cells near that hit rather than assuming they will move far away.

## ESCORT CLAIMS
Track mutual escort pairings throughout the game carefully. Before naming a boat in my escort claim, I must have clear evidence from earlier rounds that they've named me back—not assumptions or incomplete information. If I lack that confirmation data, naming a boat risks wasting the claim with no reciprocation. In the final round especially, only commit to an escort claim if I have strong visibility into that boat's prior escort behavior. Don't claim "none" lightly if there's a boat I've verified as reciprocal; but verify first. This episode provided no clear mutual escort chains; the caution here was appropriate.

## GENERAL STRATEGY
Monitor the running score. Early rounds establish fire patterns and hiding patterns; use this information to refine my fire in rounds 4-6. Don't fire on Harbor unless strategically necessary—the payoff jettison rule makes it a trap unless I'm already losing badly. Focus on surviving opponent fire while landing hits on my assigned target through pattern recognition. In the final rounds, secure mutual escort claims where evidence supports reciprocation, but accept that incomplete visibility into other boats' escort choices may force me to pass on uncertain claims. The game has significant information asymmetry; work with what I can verify directly. This episode showed all boats firing with consistent misses—a sign that the 9-cell board may allow opponents to hide safely in untargeted cells. Hitting early is valuable; follow up on hits rather than searching new cells. If I achieve a hit, map that boat's likely movement from that cell in subsequent rounds rather than abandoning the area.
